mcqs.question: Why does `obj.field` cost more in a dynamically-typed language than in a statically-typed one, all else equal?
options: Dynamically-typed languages don't support property access syntax

The statically-typed compiler knows the object's exact layout ahead of time and compiles a fixed-offset read; the dynamic runtime must handle the possibility the type or shape varies at that call site
Property access is always implemented as a network call in dynamic languages
Dynamically-typed languages store all data as strings
mcqs.explanation: A static compiler can prove the object's type and therefore its memory layout ahead of time; a dynamic runtime can't make that assumption without observing behavior first, so it pays extra lookup cost per access unless something like V8's hidden classes recovers the static-like guarantee. The other options aren't accurate descriptions of either kind of runtime.

mcqs.question: Two JavaScript objects are created with the same properties added in a different order: `{x:1, y:2}` vs `{y:2, x:1}`. What's the likely V8 consequence?
options: No consequence — V8 always normalizes property order before assigning a hidden class
They may end up with different hidden classes, defeating the shared fast-path a call site would otherwise get
V8 throws a runtime error because object shapes must match exactly
Both objects are always demoted to megamorphic call sites immediately
mcqs.explanation: Hidden classes are built from the actual sequence of property additions, so a different construction order can produce a different hidden class even with identical final properties — a real, easy-to-hit performance pitfall. V8 doesn't normalize order, doesn't throw an error over it, and a single differing object doesn't automatically make a call site megamorphic.

mcqs.question: A property-access call site in V8 has seen five different hidden classes over its lifetime. What state is its inline cache likely in?
options: Monomorphic, since inline caches only track the most recent hidden class
Uninitialized, since inline caches reset after five distinct shapes
Megamorphic, having given up on caching and fallen back to slower generic lookup
Still polymorphic, since five is within V8's tracked limit
mcqs.explanation: Once a call site sees too many distinct shapes it exceeds what an inline cache usefully tracks and becomes megamorphic, falling back to generic lookup on every access. Monomorphic caches track more than just the most recent shape (they'd have failed already), and inline caches don't simply reset after a fixed count.

mcqs.question: What is the most accurate description of how CPython, by default, executes Python attribute access?
options: It compiles the whole program to native code ahead of time, like a statically-typed AOT compiler
It uses V8-style hidden classes to give every object a fixed memory layout
It typically performs a dictionary lookup on the object's `__dict__`, without shape inference or inline caching by default
It always resolves attribute access at compile time before the program runs
mcqs.explanation: CPython's default object model backs most attribute access with a dictionary lookup rather than a fixed-offset read, historically without the shape-inference machinery V8 uses. It doesn't AOT-compile the whole program, doesn't use hidden classes, and can't resolve dynamic attribute access at compile time.

mcqs.question: What is the primary reason CPython uses a Global Interpreter Lock rather than fine-grained locking throughout the interpreter?
options: The GIL makes reference counting simple and fast to implement without needing atomic operations on every increment/decrement
Python's syntax requires a single global lock to parse correctly
The GIL is required by the operating system for any interpreted language
Multi-threading is impossible in any interpreted language without a GIL
mcqs.explanation: The GIL exists largely as a historical simplicity/performance trade for CPython's reference-counting memory model, avoiding the overhead of atomic operations on every refcount change. It's not an OS or syntax requirement, and other interpreted-language runtimes (including PyPy in some configurations, and V8 for JS) don't need an equivalent lock for the same reason.

mcqs.question: A CPU-bound Python function is spread across 4 `threading.Thread` instances on an 8-core machine. What speedup should you expect?
options: Roughly 4x, matching the thread count
Little to none — the GIL means only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound work doesn't parallelize this way
Exactly 8x, matching the core count
Threads always crash CPython when running CPU-bound code
mcqs.explanation: Because the GIL allows only one thread to run Python bytecode at any instant, CPU-bound work spread across threads takes turns rather than running in parallel — the fix is multiprocessing or a GIL-releasing C extension, not more threads. There's no crash, and neither 4x nor 8x speedup is realistic for CPU-bound Python threading.
